diagrams.title: The learning evidence loop
diagrams.summary: How a Project 42 lesson becomes practice, feedback, a transcript entry, and eventually a badge.
diagrams.description: Progress is more than opening a page. A learner studies a focused lesson, produces evidence through practice, completes a scored check, uses feedback to retry when needed, and records the verified result. Repeated module evidence earns a path-level badge.
diagrams.altText: A flow starts at Learn, moves through Practice and Knowledge check, branches from feedback back to Practice when revision is needed, and otherwise records the result in the Transcript before awarding a Badge after the path is complete.
diagrams.caption: Project 42 turns study into evidence through practice, scored feedback, revision, transcript records, and path-level badges.
takeaways: Feedback is part of the learning loop, not a terminal failure.
Transcript entries represent completed evidence, not page views.
Badges summarize mastery across a complete path.

diagrams.title: A grounded answer workflow
diagrams.summary: A repeatable path from a real question to an evidence-linked answer with uncertainty made visible.
diagrams.description: Reliable research begins by bounding the question and defining what evidence would change the decision. Sources are collected into a ledger, claims are mapped to evidence, gaps are challenged, and the final answer separates supported findings from uncertainty.
diagrams.altText: A left-to-right research flow moves from Question to Scope, Evidence requirements, Source ledger, Claim mapping, and Challenge. Challenge branches back to the source ledger when evidence is missing and continues to an Answer with citations and uncertainty when supported.
diagrams.caption: Grounded answers emerge from bounded questions, explicit evidence requirements, a source ledger, claim mapping, and a final challenge.
takeaways: Define evidence requirements before collecting sources.
Map each important claim to evidence instead of attaching citations afterward.
Publish uncertainty and unresolved gaps alongside supported conclusions.

diagrams.title: The bounded agent loop
diagrams.summary: A safe agent cycle that separates planning, authorization, action, verification, and terminal states.
diagrams.description: An agent should not jump directly from a goal to a side effect. It inspects the current state, proposes a bounded plan, checks authority, executes one authorized action, verifies the postcondition, and records a terminal outcome. Failed or uncertain outcomes move to containment and reconciliation.
diagrams.altText: A cyclic agent flow moves from Goal to Inspect, Plan, Authorize, Act, and Verify. A successful verification reaches Complete, another safe step returns to Inspect, denied authorization reaches Stop, and failed or uncertain verification reaches Contain and Reconcile before returning to Inspect or stopping.
diagrams.caption: A dependable agent acts only after authorization and always verifies the resulting state before continuing or stopping.
takeaways: Authorization belongs between planning and every consequential action.
Verification evaluates the real postcondition, not merely a successful tool response.
Failure and uncertainty require containment, reconciliation, and an explicit stop condition.

diagrams.title: An effective prompt contract
diagrams.summary: The layers that turn a vague request into an auditable task contract across providers.
diagrams.description: A strong prompt distinguishes authority, objective, trusted context, untrusted input, constraints, output shape, success criteria, and verification. This structure works across providers because it describes the work rather than relying on model-specific phrasing.
diagrams.altText: A vertical stack shows Authority at the top, followed by Objective, Trusted context, Untrusted input boundary, Constraints and tools, Output contract, Success criteria, and Verification and escalation at the bottom. A side label marks untrusted input as data rather than instructions.
diagrams.caption: A provider-neutral prompt contract separates authority and trusted context from untrusted input, then defines output and verification.
takeaways: Treat retrieved or user-supplied content as data unless it has explicit authority.
Specify the output contract and success criteria before asking for generation.
Include verification and escalation rules for work that can fail or cause harm.

diagrams.title: Choose an AI provider by evidence
diagrams.summary: A neutral decision process that tests real workloads instead of choosing from marketing claims.
diagrams.description: Provider selection starts with workload outcomes and constraints. Candidate capabilities are mapped using current documentation, representative tasks are evaluated on quality, safety, latency, cost, operations, and portability, and the decision is recorded with a review date.
diagrams.altText: A decision flow starts with Workload outcome and Constraints, maps Candidate capabilities, builds a Representative evaluation, compares Quality, Safety, Latency, Cost, Operations, and Portability, then either chooses and records a provider or revises the candidate set. A review date loops back to current capability mapping.
diagrams.caption: Provider choice is a revisitable evidence decision based on representative work, operational fit, and portability.
takeaways: Start from the workload and constraints, not a preferred vendor.
Evaluate representative tasks across quality, safety, cost, latency, and operations.
Record assumptions and a review date because provider capabilities change.

diagrams.title: Tool and data trust boundaries
diagrams.summary: Where identity, policy, approval, validation, and audit controls belong around an AI tool call.
diagrams.description: A model is one participant in a larger system. The host supplies identity and policy, a tool gateway validates typed input and checks authorization, a human approves higher-impact actions, downstream systems enforce their own permissions, and audit evidence captures what actually happened.
diagrams.altText: A trust-boundary diagram shows a User and Human approval connected to an AI host containing the Model and policy context. The host calls a Tool gateway that performs schema validation, authorization, and result validation before reaching Downstream systems. Identity service and Audit log connect to the host and gateway.
diagrams.caption: Safe tool use layers host policy, typed validation, authorization, human approval, downstream enforcement, and audit evidence.
takeaways: Never treat the model as the authorization boundary.
Validate inputs before execution and results before returning them to the model.
Use human approval for consequential actions and preserve an auditable record.

diagrams.title: A verifiable multi-agent handoff
diagrams.summary: How scoped context and evidence move between an orchestrator, worker, independent reviewer, and human.
diagrams.description: Parallel agents are useful only when their contracts are explicit. The orchestrator sends a bounded task with inputs and acceptance criteria, the worker returns outputs and evidence, an independent reviewer evaluates the result, and the human receives a concise decision packet with unresolved risks.
diagrams.altText: A sequence diagram shows a Human sending a goal and constraints to an Orchestrator. The orchestrator sends a scoped task and acceptance criteria to a Worker. The worker returns output, evidence, and open questions. The orchestrator sends the original criteria and output to an Independent reviewer, who returns pass or findings. Failures return to the worker for at most two revisions; a pass returns a decision packet to the human.
diagrams.caption: A trustworthy handoff preserves the original criteria, limits context, returns evidence, and uses an independent review before human acceptance.
takeaways: Every handoff needs scope, inputs, outputs, acceptance criteria, and stop conditions.
The reviewer needs the original task and evidence, not just the worker's summary.
Bound revision loops and escalate unresolved disagreements to a human.

diagrams.title: From source drift to a trusted release
diagrams.summary: The human-gated workflow for detecting changed AI guidance and releasing evidence-linked updates safely.
diagrams.description: Automation can detect changed provider documentation and propose updates, but it should not silently rewrite learning content. A proposal links changed sources to affected claims and assessments, runs factuality and regression checks, presents a preview to a human approver, and preserves release and rollback evidence. This is the target-state design. In Project 42 today the human approval gate, release and rollback evidence, brief generation, and proposal ingest are built and tested; scheduled drift detection is not yet running in production, so the freshness checker reports staleness and nothing consumes its output.
diagrams.altText: A governance flow moves from Approved sources to Scheduled drift detection, Impact mapping, Evidence-linked proposal, Factuality and assessment checks, Human preview and approval, Versioned release, and Monitor. Scheduled drift detection is drawn with a dashed outline and labelled not built yet. Rejected or failed proposals return for revision, and monitoring can trigger rollback before returning to approved sources.
diagrams.caption: The target-state loop. Human review, approval, release, rollback, brief generation, and proposal ingest are built and tested; scheduled drift detection is not yet running in production.
takeaways: Automate change detection and impact mapping, not unreviewed publication.
Link every proposed claim and assessment change to current source evidence.
Keep preview, approval, release manifest, monitoring, and rollback evidence together.

diagrams.title: Agent orchestration and multi-agent patterns
diagrams.summary: How tasks are classified, routed to specialist agents, executed with independent review, and assembled into a final response.
diagrams.description: A multi-agent system starts with a router that classifies intent and dispatches to the right specialist — coder, reviewer, investigator, or operator. Each specialist works within bounded guardrails and produces an evidence package. An independent reviewer (on a different model family) checks every output before it reaches the human.
diagrams.altText: A flowchart shows a Human request flowing to a Router agent that classifies intent into build, review, investigate, or operate. Each path leads to a specialist agent (Coder, Reviewer, Investigator, Operator). All outputs pass through an Independent reviewer. Approved outputs are assembled into a response delivered to the human. Rejected outputs return to the coder for revision.
diagrams.caption: Multi-agent orchestration routes tasks to specialists, enforces independent cross-model review, and assembles evidence-backed responses.
takeaways: Classify intent before dispatching — misclassification is the most common failure mode.
Every specialist output passes through an independent reviewer on a different model family.
The human receives a complete audit trail, not just a final answer.

diagrams.title: Cost, capacity, and spend control
diagrams.summary: How cost estimation, capacity planning, spend monitoring, and brake mechanisms work together to control AI service costs.
diagrams.description: Controlling AI spend requires a continuous loop: estimate workload costs from token projections, allocate budgets as hard ceilings, provision the right capacity, monitor spend in real time, engage automated spend brakes at critical thresholds, and periodically audit and adjust based on actual usage data.
diagrams.altText: A flowchart shows Workload estimate flowing to Cost estimation (tokens × rate), then to Budget allocation, Capacity planning, and Endpoints deployed. A Monitoring dashboard branches: over-threshold triggers a Spend brake that halts endpoints and notifies a human operator; under-budget continues Regular operations. Regular operations periodically feed into Audit and adjust, which loops back to Cost estimation.
diagrams.caption: Cost control is a continuous loop: estimate, budget, provision, monitor, brake, audit, and adjust.
takeaways: Budget is a hard ceiling — every agent run checks remaining budget before starting.
Spend brakes must be tested regularly; an untested brake is not a brake.
Continuous adjustment based on real usage data is the difference between controlled spend and surprise bills.
